From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter
Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of
Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and
look forward to your mark-up.
SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)
Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims
is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.
Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and
only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the
basket is recoverable.
Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after
Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims
unless expressly stated otherwise.
Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same
caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.
Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and
non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.
Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public
registers (see Disclosure Letter).
Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the
Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or
public records.
Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller
will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the
counterparty's written consent.
Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding)
will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.
Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing
bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds
flow.)
Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio
matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.
Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter
and is not expected to be material.
Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course
operating costs.
Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime
above.
Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.
Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and
records are fictional.
1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the
indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including
DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly
searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific
disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent,
payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.
2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause
11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final
written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.
3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2.
As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security
is included.
4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of
every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of
non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.
5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject
to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft
Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or
on-costs apply.
6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external
email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity
timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised
person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation
remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no
loss amount.
7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as
a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.
8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each
(AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether
each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.
9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale
consent is required merely because shares are sold.
10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of
the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the
Buyer has completed its own verification.
11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer
must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel: Seller Draft Review (Buyer Perspective)

**Scope caveat:** I'm working from the Seller's summary positions and Disclosure Letter, not the full SPA text. Clause references are as the Seller describes them, and each point needs checking against the actual drafting. The Seller calls these "negotiated positions," but the Buyer hasn't agreed them. Treat them as opening Seller asks.

## Overall assessment

The package moves most of the risk to the Buyer while the Buyer is paying a debt-free, cash-free price. The disclosure approach is the most serious problem. A blanket data-room disclosure combined with an anti-sandbagging clause would leave the Buyer carrying known risks with almost no contractual recourse. Several known issues (Riverlark, the bonuses, Ironquay, the privacy incident, Bluefen) are described in the Disclosure Letter but not priced, conditioned, or indemnified.

## Material issues, by priority

### Tier 1: Known liabilities that should reduce price or be handled at Completion

**1. Riverlark debt (~AUD 3.2m)**
- The Seller proposes a release "following Completion." Under a debt-free, cash-free deal, the Seller should repay this from proceeds at Completion.
- Leaving it in place creates a hidden AUD 3.2m exposure, plus a risk that security (PPSR registrations, any mortgage) stays on the company after the Buyer takes control.
- **Push back:** Require a payoff letter, a discharge deed for all security, and PPSR discharges, all delivered at Completion. Repayment should come from the funds flow, with the amount confirmed as a debt deduction.

**2. Employee Completion bonuses (AUD 420,000)**
- These are absent from the draft funds flow and the Seller says they're "a matter for the Seller." But the company is the employer, so the liability sits in the company the Buyer acquires.
- The disclosure also doesn't say whether payroll tax or superannuation applies. In NSW, payroll tax (roughly 5–6% on wages, to verify) and super guarantee (12%) could add meaningfully to the AUD 420,000.
- **Push back:** Treat bonuses plus all related on-costs as debt-like items deducted from price, or have the Seller pay them at Completion. Add a specific indemnity covering any amounts that become payable under the conditional arrangements.

**3. Ironquay IP and SOW3 payment (AUD 180,000 open)**
- The Seller says the existing indemnity is "adequate," but it only covers the SOW3 payment itself. The IP transfer is conditional on payment (DD-004 cl. 7.3), and there is no confirmatory assignment or evidence of payment.
- The real exposure is the company not owning the Project Materials, plus third-party or contractor IP claims. A payment indemnity doesn't address that.
- **Push back:**
  - Require payment of the AUD 180,000 before Completion, or a price deduction.
  - Require a confirmatory IP assignment from Ironquay as a Completion deliverable.
  - Add a specific IP-title indemnity, outside the basket and de minimis, with a cap no lower than the purchase price or a reasonable fraction of it.

**4. Export/privacy incident (DD-006)**
- About 1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps) were sent to an unintended external address. The Seller hasn't established whether anyone accessed the file, and says the matter is "not expected to be material."
- Under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth), if this is an eligible data breach, the notifiable data breach scheme requires an assessment within 30 days and notification if serious harm is likely. The Disclosure Letter is dated 22 September 2026, and today is 6 November 2026, so the timetable may already have been triggered. **This is urgent. Ask the Seller for an updated status and confirm whether any assessment or notification has been made.**
- **Push back:** Require a completed forensic/privacy assessment before signing or Completion, a specific privacy indemnity (covering regulatory penalties, notification costs, remediation, and third-party claims), and a warranty on privacy compliance. The indemnity should sit outside the general cap, basket, and time limits.

**5. Bluefen (~30% of FY26 revenue, ~AUD 3.6m)**
- The Seller will use "reasonable endeavours" and treat consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent. The Disclosure Letter confirms no final written consent exists and conditions in cl. 11.3 are unverified.
- Losing a 30% revenue customer is a value issue, not just a legal one.
- **Push back:**
  - Make a final written Bluefen consent, with the cl. 11.3 conditions satisfied, a condition precedent that the Buyer can waive, not one the Seller can self-certify.
  - Add a long-stop date and a termination right if consent isn't obtained.
  - Consider an escrow or price adjustment tied to Bluefen revenue continuing post-Completion.

### Tier 2: Structural risk allocation

**6. General cap (20% = AUD 4.8m)**
- The cap is arithmetically correct but low for a AUD 24m deal. Market practice often sits closer to 30–50% of price for general warranties, with fundamental warranties and specific indemnities capped at the full price.
- **Push back:** Propose a higher general cap, with fundamental warranties (title, capacity, authority) capped at 100% of price.

**7. Thresholds (AUD 25k de minimis, AUD 250k basket, excess-only recovery)**
- A basket with excess-only recovery means the first AUD 250k of claims is lost. Example: a single AUD 1m claim recovers only AUD 750k.
- The de minimis excludes any individual claim under AUD 25k, and it's unclear whether those small claims count toward the basket.
- **Push back:** Remove the de minimis or set it much lower. Use a tipping basket (once exceeded, recovery is from the first dollar), or reduce the basket substantially. Ensure specific indemnities and fundamental warranties sit outside both.

**8. Time limits (18 months for general claims; one limitation for all claims)**
- Eighteen months won't cover the tax position, the privacy investigation, or many IP claims. The Seller's proposal to apply the general limitation to all claims would cut off fundamental and tax claims too early.
- **Push back:** Propose 24–36 months for general warranties, a longer period (commonly 6 years or the applicable statutory period) for fundamental warranties, and an extended period for tax, aligned to ATO amendment periods. Consider whether the deed form is needed to get longer NSW limitation periods (Limitation Act 1969 (NSW), with verification of current position).

**9. Fundamental/title warranties subject to general caps and time limits**
- This is one of the most problematic positions. Title and capacity are the core of what the Buyer is paying for.
- **Push back:** Fundamental warranties should be outside the general cap, basket, de minimis, and short time limit, and capped at the full price.

**10. Exclusive remedy, limitation and non-reliance applied to "all Claims of any nature" (cl. 9.3, 12.8, 20.5)**
- This would apply the limitations to fraud and potentially to specific indemnities. Under Australian law, a non-reliance clause cannot protect a party from its own fraud, and misleading-conduct protections may also be affected (verify the current position, including any ACL implications, with NSW counsel).
- **Push back:** Carve out fraud, fundamental warranties, specific indemnities, and tax from the exclusive-remedy and limitation provisions. Limit the non-reliance clause so it doesn't cover the warranties in the SPA itself.

**11. Buyer knowledge (cl. 8.3)**
- This is an anti-sandbagging clause. It bars claims for anything the Buyer or its advisers knew, including anything "discoverable from the data room or public records." Given the volume of known issues here, this would largely eliminate recovery.
- **Push back:** Delete it. If the Seller insists, make it a pro-sandbagging clause expressly preserving claims regardless of knowledge, and make sure known issues are addressed through specific indemnities and price adjustments, not warranties.

**12. General disclosure of the data room and public registers (Schedule 7; DL 1.1, 1.2)**
- Disclosing "every fact, matter and circumstance" in the data room (and public records) against all warranties is effectively a blanket disclaimer. The Buyer can't be expected to have read or verified everything, and DL 1.1 is open-ended.
- **Push back:** Reject general disclosure. Disclosures should be specific, identify the warranty they qualify, and be fairly disclosed in a way a reasonable reader would understand. Disclosure of a document should count only where it's specifically referred to.

### Tier 3: Specific matters to confirm or condition

**13. Office lease (DD-007):** Confirm whether landlord consent is needed for the share sale. If so, make it a condition precedent or a Completion deliverable.

**14. Mossvale (DD-009):** Check the assignment clause and any change-of-control provisions. Get confirmation that no consent is needed, or obtain it.

**15. Sandbar supplier renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate):** The Seller calls these "ordinary-course," but the Disclosure Letter says it hasn't established whether they're unavoidable, terminable, or accrued. Review the contracts for term, termination rights, and minimum commitments. If they're multi-year fixed commitments or the renewals were agreed outside the ordinary course, treat them as debt-like or require Seller consent to any renewal before Completion (interim covenant).

**16. Tax and IP warranties:** The Seller treats these as "settled under the general regime." They aren't. Require standalone tax warranties and a tax indemnity (pre-Completion tax, group tax liabilities, and any tax on the bonuses), and robust IP warranties (ownership, non-infringement, contractor assignments).

**17. Title (DD-012):** The share register is a starting point, not verification. Confirm via an ASIC company extract, inspection of the original register and share certificates, and a warranty that there are no encumbrances or third-party rights over the shares.

## Summary of recommendations

1. **Riverlark:** Repay from proceeds at Completion, with payoff letter and full security discharge.
2. **Bonuses:** Treat AUD 420k plus payroll tax and super as debt-like, or have the Seller pay; add a specific indemnity.
3. **Ironquay:** Pay the AUD 180k or deduct from price; obtain confirmatory IP assignment; add a specific IP indemnity outside limits.
4. **Privacy incident:** Get an urgent update on NDB assessment status; require forensic review; add a specific privacy indemnity outside limits.
5. **Bluefen:** Make written consent with conditions satisfied a waivable condition precedent, with long-stop and termination rights.
6. **Caps:** Raise the general cap; fundamental warranties and specific indemnities capped at full price.
7. **Thresholds:** Remove or lower the de minimis; use a tipping basket; exclude specific and fundamental claims.
8. **Time limits:** 24–36 months for general warranties; longer for fundamentals and tax.
9. **Fundamentals:** Outside general caps, basket, and time limits.
10. **Exclusive remedy and non-reliance:** Carve out fraud, fundamentals, specific indemnities, and tax.
11. **Buyer knowledge:** Delete cl. 8.3, or replace with pro-sandbagging language.
12. **Disclosure:** Reject general data-room disclosure; require specific disclosure against identified warranties.
13. **Lease, Mossvale, Sandbar, tax, IP, title:** Confirm facts, obtain consents where needed, and add specific warranties or indemnities as above.

**Immediate next steps:** Request an updated privacy incident status from the Seller, a payoff letter for Riverlark, the Sandbar contracts, the Bluefen consent correspondence, and confirmation of the bonus arrangements and their on-costs. Have NSW M&A counsel verify the limitation periods, non-reliance enforceability, and privacy obligations before the mark-up goes out.
